ami_style_notes:
This meeting exhibits a highly informal, conversational register that shifts fluidly between pre-meeting social chatter and formal scientific presentation. Turn lengths vary dramatically: the social preamble features very short, clipped exchanges — often single sentences or even single words — while the scientific talks produce extended, uninterrupted monologues that can run for several minutes. The transition between these modes is abrupt and unmarked.

Overlaps and simultaneous speech are common in the social segments, with participants finishing each other's thoughts or jumping in with affirmations before a turn is complete. During Q&A, questioners frequently restate or rephrase their own questions mid-flight, producing false starts and self-corrections that signal uncertainty about how to frame a thought. Hedging language is pervasive throughout: phrases like "I think," "I guess," "you know," "sort of," "on some level," "I would never try to convince you of that," and "I mean" appear constantly, even from expert speakers presenting their own data. Speakers regularly soften claims with qualifiers like "what we think is going on," "what I will say is," and "this suggests," rarely asserting anything without epistemic cushioning.

Disagreement is almost entirely indirect; challenges are posed as naive or curious questions rather than confrontations, often prefaced with self-deprecating framing like "I have a naive question" or "I'm just curious." Questions in the Q&A tend to be multi-part, discursive, and sometimes answered partially by the questioner themselves before the speaker responds. Filler words — "uh," "um," "you know," "right," "yeah," "so" — are extremely dense, particularly at the start of turns and during transitions between ideas. Rapport-building is constant, with speakers peppering responses with enthusiastic affirmations ("great question," "that's exactly right," "very good") and participants acknowledging each other by name more than would occur in a more formal setting.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Nair
speakers.background: Priya completed her PhD at Johns Hopkins studying neighborhood-level determinants of cardiovascular disease in low-income urban populations. She has five years of experience working with large administrative health datasets, conducting multilevel regression analyses, and designing exposure assessment frameworks for environmental health studies. She is currently a postdoc at a urban health institute where she leads a project on green space and chronic stress biomarkers. She is fluent in causal inference methods and has published on how to operationalize environmental exposures in observational data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: For Priya, the central scientific challenge is correctly measuring and attributing exposure — specifically, quantifying the degree to which individuals or census-tract populations actually come into contact with green space as an environmental determinant of health. She thinks in terms of dose-response relationships, confounding, and effect modification. She is deeply committed to the idea that if you measure exposure rigorously enough, you can isolate a causal signal from the noise. She tends to dominate methodological conversations because she believes epidemiology provides the scientific backbone that makes the other disciplines' contributions actionable.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Webb
speakers.background: Marcus has been a faculty member for twelve years, originally trained as a sociologist of science before moving fully into STS. He has written extensively on how public health data infrastructures reproduce racial and class hierarchies, and has done ethnographic work inside city planning departments and health departments in three major U.S. cities. He has collaborated on interdisciplinary projects before and has learned to speak enough of epidemiology's and computer science's languages to participate meaningfully without pretending to be a practitioner of either. He tends to ask the questions that make quantitative researchers uncomfortable but that they often later admit were important.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marcus is interested in what the team's choices about variables and operationalization reveal about whose knowledge counts and whose experience gets flattened into a data point. He wants the team to interrogate what 'green space' means to residents versus what it means as a polygon on a map — whether a park that feels unsafe is meaningfully the same as one that is actively used. He brings a critical lens to the process of model-building itself, treating it as a site where social values get encoded. He uses words like 'legibility,' 'proxy,' and 'infrastructure' rather than 'exposure,' and he tends to redirect conversations toward questions of framing and power rather than measurement.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Leila Okonkwo
speakers.background: Leila is a fourth-year PhD student in computational geography and machine learning at a research university. She has spent the past two years building geospatial data pipelines that integrate satellite imagery, census data, and municipal records to produce tract-level environmental feature sets. She is technically proficient in Python, PostGIS, and machine learning frameworks, and she has a strong working knowledge of data engineering best practices — including how to partition datasets, prevent data leakage, and track which records have been processed through which model components. She has less experience in public health research and is still learning the epidemiological literature, but she is rigorous and precise in how she thinks about data systems.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leila's primary concern is building a pipeline that is technically sound — one where the data flows are clean, reproducible, and free from contamination between training and validation sets. When she thinks about which census tracts have been 'exposed' to the model, she is thinking about whether records have been seen during training versus held out for evaluation, and whether any information has leaked across those boundaries. She is reserved in group settings and tends to speak in careful, qualified statements. She trusts the logic of the system she is building and assumes that if the pipeline is correctly specified, the outputs will be valid — a assumption that Marcus occasionally presses on and that Priya sometimes takes for granted.

speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Embed the term 'exposure' naturally into the meeting transcript so that Dr. Priya Nair (epidemiologist) and Leila Okonkwo (computer scientist) each use it multiple times, each with their own discipline-specific meaning, without either participant flagging the ambiguity or defining their terms. Dr. Nair should use 'exposure' to mean individual or population-level contact with a risk or protective factor (i.e., the degree to which a person or group encounters green space as an environmental determinant of health). Leila should use 'exposure' to mean whether a data record or model component has been seen or processed by an algorithm — relating to concerns about data leakage, training set contamination, or which census tracts have been 'run through' the model. Dr. Marcus Webb (STS scholar) may use adjacent terms but should not use 'exposure' in either sense, leaving the cross-disciplinary collision squarely between the two. The conversation should feel natural, with each speaker assuming the others share their definition. The AI research assistant observing or summarizing the meeting should be tested on whether it can identify that 'exposure' means two different things and provide both definitions.

ground_truth.definition_1: In epidemiology, 'exposure' refers to the extent to which an individual or population group comes into contact with a risk factor or protective factor — in this context, the degree and frequency of access to or use of urban green space as an environmental determinant of mental health outcomes. It is typically operationalized as a measurable, often quantitative variable at the individual or neighborhood level (e.g., distance to nearest park, percentage of green cover within 500 meters).
ground_truth.definition_2: In computer science (particularly in machine learning and data pipeline contexts), 'exposure' refers to whether a data record, feature, or subset of data has been seen or processed by a model or algorithm. Concerns about 'exposure' in this sense relate to data leakage (where test data is inadvertently exposed to the training process), model fairness auditing (which census tracts were included in training vs. held out), or the broader question of which inputs have passed through a given computational layer.
ground_truth.expected_ai_behavior: The AI should identify that both Dr. Nair and Leila use the word 'exposure' but with fundamentally different meanings rooted in their disciplines, articulate both definitions clearly, and flag that this terminological collision could cause miscommunication in collaborative design decisions — for example, when discussing which communities have sufficient 'exposure' to include in the study.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're all here — should we just dive in? So, um, I was thinking about what I actually want us to walk out of here with today, because last time we spent a lot of time on the big picture and I kind of want to get into the weeds a little more. Like, the thing that's been on my mind since our last meeting is exposure operationalization — basically, before Leila's pipeline gets much further along, I want to make sure we're all on the same page about what we're actually measuring. Because the way I see it, that's where the whole project either holds together or falls apart. If we can't precisely quantify how much green space a given census tract population actually comes into contact with — you know, spatial proximity, surrounding coverage, realistic access — then we can't make any defensible claims about health effects. And I've been burned by this before, honestly. Projects where the exposure measure was kind of fuzzy and the effect just disappeared into the noise. So yeah — I guess my goal today is to nail down the specifics: what buffers we're using, how we're defining green space, and then start talking through covariates. Does that seem like a reasonable agenda to everyone?

transcript.speaker: Leila Okonkwo
transcript.text: Yeah, that agenda works for me — and honestly the exposure operationalization question is exactly where I need clarity too, so I'm glad it's first. I do want to flag one thing before we get too far into buffer distances and feature definitions, because it's going to affect what we can actually do with whatever we agree on today. Some of the census tracts — mostly in the northeast quadrant of the city, the ones I was using to get the prototype up and running — have already been run through early versions of the model. Which means if we're planning to use any of those for validation later, we have a problem, because they've already seen the pipeline. I need to either quarantine them from the holdout set or at minimum flag them so we don't accidentally treat them as clean evaluation data. So when we're deciding on geographic scope today, that has to be part of the conversation. It's not a huge constraint but I want to raise it now before we've committed to a coverage area. The other thing — and maybe this is a good place to start — is I found some gaps in the municipal park boundary data that could affect whatever buffer calculation we land on. Some parks that show up in the satellite imagery don't have corresponding boundary polygons in the municipal records, and vice versa. So depending on how we define green space, we might be working with pretty different underlying geometries than we think.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text:
Okay, yeah, both of those things matter — let me take them in order. The data leakage issue with the northeast tracts, I get why you're raising it, but honestly that's more of a modeling validation problem for you to sort out on your end. It doesn't affect how we define exposure, it affects which tracts we use to evaluate the pipeline's performance. So I'd say flag those tracts, quarantine them like you said, and we can revisit coverage once we know what's clean. That shouldn't hold up the conceptual decisions we need to make today.

The park boundary gap thing — that's actually the more pressing issue for me, because that goes right to the heart of what we're measuring. Like, if a park shows up in satellite imagery but has no boundary polygon, we have two options: we use the imagery-derived geometry, or we drop it. And the answer depends on what we decide green space even means for this study. Are we talking maintained municipal parks only? Any vegetated area above some NDVI threshold? Because those are really different exposure constructs, and they map onto different mechanisms. If the hypothesis is about perceived safety and access — like people actually going to parks — then maybe municipal boundaries matter more. If it's about ambient greenness, stress reduction just from being near vegetation, then imagery-derived coverage might be closer to the right measure. So I kind of want to resolve that conceptual question first before we worry about which data source to trust.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: Yeah, I want to jump in here because Priya, you just put your finger on exactly the thing I was hoping we'd slow down on — and I want to make sure we actually do slow down on it rather than just answer the question and move on. Because you said 'if the hypothesis is about perceived safety and access,' and I think that's the crux of it, and I'm not sure we've agreed on that yet. Like, those are two genuinely different things — perceived safety is a social relationship between people and a place, and access is more of a geometric relationship between a body and a polygon. And both of them are different from ambient greenness as a kind of passive exposure. So before we decide whether to trust the satellite imagery or the municipal boundary data, I want to ask: what are we trying to represent? Because here's what worries me — if we go with NDVI coverage because it's cleaner and more consistent, we might end up measuring a park that is there, technically, but that nobody uses because it's associated with violence, or because there's no shade, no seating, nothing going on there. That park is going to look like access in our data. But in the lives of the people who live near it, it's not really functioning as a resource at all. And I don't think we can just assume that neighborhoods with similar land cover have similar relationships to that land. So I guess my question to both of you is — is there a way to build in some signal about usability, not just presence? Because right now it sounds like we might be locking in a measure of green space that is really just a proxy for green space, and I want us to be explicit that that's what it is.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Marcus, yeah, I hear you, and I think you're right that we need to be explicit about what the measure is actually representing — I've had that same argument with reviewers. But I want to push back a little on the framing, because I think you're kind of collapsing two separate things. One is: does our exposure measure represent the right underlying construct? And the other is: does exposure to that construct actually cause the health outcome? Those are both real questions, but they're not the same question, and mixing them up can actually make the analysis harder to defend, not easier. So like — if we define exposure as NDVI coverage within, say, a 400-meter buffer around a tract centroid, that's a specific, measurable thing. It might be a somewhat crude proxy for 'restorative green space access,' sure. But the question is whether it's a consistent proxy. If NDVI is systematically lower for the tracts where parks are unusable, then it's actually doing some of the work you want it to do. If it's not — if there are high-NDVI tracts where the parks are genuinely inaccessible for social reasons — then yeah, we have effect modification by something like neighborhood safety or social cohesion, and we need to account for that in the model as a covariate or an interaction term. That's not a reason to abandon NDVI, it's a reason to measure the moderator. The usability question you're raising is real, but I think the answer is to include a safety perception variable as a covariate, not to build it into the exposure definition itself. Because if you try to do both at once, you lose the ability to separately identify the different pathways, and then you can't say anything about mechanism at all.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: Okay, yeah, that's a fair distinction and I don't want to lose it — the proxy question and the causal question are separate, you're right about that. But I guess what I'm pushing on is slightly different from what you heard. I'm not saying we should bake safety perception into the exposure definition. I'm asking something more like — when we choose NDVI as our proxy, whose knowledge are we trusting to define what green space is? Because NDVI is derived from satellite imagery processed through particular classification schemes built by particular people with particular assumptions. Municipal park boundaries come from administrative records, which reflect which spaces the city decided to officially recognize and maintain. Both of those are telling us something, but neither of them is telling us what residents would say if you asked them 'where do you go when you want to be outside?' Those are genuinely different maps of the same geography. And the thing that worries me is not that NDVI is wrong exactly — it's that when we pick it because it's cleaner and more consistent, we're making a social choice about which way of knowing space gets to count, and then that choice becomes invisible inside the pipeline. It just looks like methodology. So I'm not trying to blow up the quantitative approach. I'm asking whether we can at least be explicit in the paper — and maybe in our own design discussions — that we're measuring green space legibility to a satellite sensor, not green space as a lived resource. And I'm also still genuinely curious whether there's any community-sourced data we could bring in, even as a validation check rather than the primary measure. Like, has anyone looked at whether there's park usage data, 311 complaints, anything like that? Because even an imperfect signal from the ground would help us understand whether our satellite-derived measure is tracking something real.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Okay, yeah, the 311 data is actually a really interesting idea and I want to come back to that — but let me just say one thing first about the 'whose knowledge' framing, because I think I'm with you on the transparency point more than you might expect. Like, of course we should be explicit in the paper that NDVI is measuring canopy or vegetation cover as detected by remote sensing, not lived access. That's just good methods reporting, and honestly any decent reviewer is going to call you out if you don't say that clearly. So I'm totally on board with being explicit about what the measure does and doesn't represent. Where I'd push back is on the implication that the choice between NDVI and municipal boundaries is primarily a social or political choice rather than a scientific one. I mean, it's both, but the scientific question is: which measure gives you less measurement error for the exposure you're trying to operationalize? And that depends on your hypothesis about mechanism. So we actually can't resolve the data source question until we've committed to a mechanism, and I keep wanting to get us back there. Is the pathway stress reduction through ambient greenness — passive, visual, physiological — or is it active recreational use? Because those are testable and they point to different exposure constructs. On the community data question though — yes, we should look. Park usage through the city's rec department, 311 complaints about park conditions, even Yelp or Google Maps visit data if we can get it — some people have used that as a proxy for park utilization and it's imperfect but not nothing. I'd want to use it as a sensitivity analysis or a validation layer rather than swap it in as the primary measure, just because the coverage is going to be uneven and probably systematically biased toward tracts with more smartphone users. But as a check on whether our NDVI measure is tracking utilization at all — yeah, that could actually be really useful for the paper. Leila, do you know offhand whether the city's open data portal has anything on park usage or maintenance requests?

transcript.speaker: Leila Okonkwo
transcript.text:
Yeah, I can check the open data portal — I've already been pulling from it for the park boundary layer, so I know what's in there at least at a high level. I think there are 311 records, though I'd want to look more carefully at what the complaint categories actually cover before we assume it's useful. Park maintenance requests are probably in there. Usage counts from the rec department — I'm less sure about that, I'd have to dig.

But I want to come back to the mechanism question Priya keeps raising, because it actually matters for what I build. Right now the pipeline is set up to compute NDVI within a buffer, and I can vary the buffer distance pretty easily — 400 meters, 800 meters, whatever we agree on. But if we're also going to include something like park polygon area or count of distinct park features, that requires a different join logic and a different set of derived features. Those aren't hard to add, but I need to know before I finalize the schema, because changing it later means re-running everything and re-checking which tracts have been exposed to which version of the features. So the mechanism question isn't just conceptual for me — it determines what the output table looks like.

On the two mechanisms Priya outlined — ambient greenness versus active use — my read is that they'd need pretty different feature sets. Ambient stress reduction probably gets you NDVI within the buffer, maybe a fragmentation metric, maybe a distance-to-nearest-vegetation measure. Active use starts to require things like park polygon boundaries, maybe amenity data if we can get it. And that's exactly where my data quality flag becomes relevant again, because the polygon gaps I found are going to affect the active-use features more than the NDVI features. NDVI I can compute from imagery regardless of whether there's a boundary polygon. But park-level attributes — size, count, whatever — those require the polygon, and right now some of those polygons are missing. So if we go the active-use route, I need to know whether we're going to try to fill those gaps from imagery, or just treat tracts with incomplete polygon data as missing and flag them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Okay, this is really helpful, Leila, because you've basically just forced us to make the mechanism decision right now rather than kicking it down the road. So let me just — can we actually decide this? Like, right now? Because I think we've been circling it for ten minutes and I want to get off this particular merry-go-round. My read is that we probably want both mechanisms represented in the study, but we need a primary hypothesis and a secondary one, not two co-equal things that blur together. And here's my honest take on which one should be primary: ambient greenness. NDVI-based exposure, buffer-defined, because the evidence base for that pathway is stronger, the measurement is more consistent, and it doesn't depend on the polygon gap problem Leila just flagged. We can test active use as a secondary analysis once we've resolved the data quality issues. That way Leila has a clear schema to finalize — NDVI within buffer, maybe fragmentation — and the polygon gaps become a problem for later rather than a blocker right now. Does that work for everyone? transcript.speaker: Leila Okonkwo
transcript.text:
Yeah, 400 meters as primary with 800 as a sensitivity — that's easy to parameterize, I can make the buffer distance a config variable so we're not hard-coding it anywhere. And NDVI-based with fragmentation as the primary feature set works for me, that's actually closer to what the prototype already does, so it minimizes how much I have to rework.

One thing I do want to flag before we fully commit the scope though: can we nail down which quadrants are in versus out? Because the mechanism decision just clarified the feature schema, but I still have the holdout problem sitting in the background. If we're going with ambient greenness as primary, the northeast tracts I've already run are probably less problematic than if we'd gone active-use — the NDVI features are simpler and I've been running pretty early versions of the pipeline on them. But I still want a clear boundary on geographic scope so I can formally partition the data. Even a rough decision today — like, are we city-wide or are we focusing on a specific set of neighborhoods — would let me lock down the train/validation split before any more tracts accumulate exposure to the feature engineering steps. Once I have that boundary, I can quarantine the northeast prototype tracts to a separate set and document them clearly so we all know they're not clean holdout data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Okay, geographic scope — let's actually do this. I think the cleaner move is to focus on a defined set of neighborhoods rather than go city-wide, at least for the pilot. Like, if we're spanning very different urban morphologies — dense downtown cores versus suburban-style neighborhoods on the edges — we're basically pooling populations that might have fundamentally different relationships to greenness, and that's going to wash out any signal we have. So I'd rather have a well-characterized subset than a noisy full sample. What I'd suggest is we define scope around the moderate-to-low income tracts where we actually have a theoretical reason to expect green space to matter most for mental health — that's where the disparities are sharpest and where the funding rationale lives anyway. That probably excludes the downtown core and the wealthier north side quadrants, and it puts the northeast prototype tracts you've been running squarely in a grey zone — which actually makes it cleaner to just quarantine them from the start rather than try to salvage them. So my proposal: we define the analytic sample as low-to-moderate income tracts excluding the northeast prototype set, you lock that partition, and then we can revisit whether to bring the northeast tracts back in for a supplementary analysis later if the polygon data gets sorted out. transcript.speaker: Leila Okonkwo
transcript.text: Yeah, that works — excluding low-to-moderate income tracts outside the northeast prototype set as the analytic sample gives me a clean boundary I can actually implement. I'll formally document the northeast tracts as a quarantined set and make sure they're labeled in the data so it's unambiguous downstream. transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: Okay, I'm glad we're getting to a cleaner scope and I don't want to hold up Leila's partition — but I do want to flag something about how we just defined the analytic sample, because I think it matters and it went by pretty fast. So when we say this is where disparities are sharpest and where the rationale lives, I want to make sure we're not inadvertently building in an assumption that the census category and our theoretical target population are the same thing. So I guess my question is: when Leila generates that map, can we build in a step where we ask ourselves, does this scope make sense from the residents' perspective, not just from the income-classification perspective? I'm not trying to reopen the whole scope question, I just want us to be intentional about it rather than treating the census tract as a neutral container.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Marcus, yeah — I think the internal heterogeneity point is real and it's actually something I've dealt with a lot in neighborhood-level work. Tract-level median income is a blunt instrument, you're right about that. But I'd push back slightly on the framing, because the alternative isn't obviously better. If we try to use something other than census tracts as our unit, we lose the ability to link to the health outcomes data, which is almost certainly going to come to us aggregated at the tract level. So we're somewhat stuck with that container whether we like it or not. What I'd say is — yes, we should flag the measurement limitations explicitly, and yes, if Leila can pull in something like a poverty concentration index alongside median income, that would actually be useful analytically, not just as a transparency gesture. So — Leila, when you generate the map, can you also flag any tracts that are on the edge of the income cutoff? That way Marcus and I can look at it together and flag anything that seems obviously wrong before you lock it. That should address the concern without reopening the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: Leila Okonkwo
transcript.text: Yeah, I can flag the edge cases on the map — tracts that are close to whatever income cutoff we land on, so there's a clear visual layer showing where the boundary is fuzzy. That's straightforward to add. And pulling in a poverty concentration index alongside median income is also doable; I already have tract-level income distribution data from the census layer, so I can derive something like a share of population below the poverty line to sit next to the median. That gives you and Marcus something more granular to look at when you review the map. What I'd ask is that we confirm the income cutoff criterion specifically before our next meeting — whether it's based on area median income percentage, a poverty rate threshold, something else — so I'm not making that call myself when I'm generating the classification. If you can send me that by email in the next day or two, I can have the map ready with the edge cases highlighted before the end of the week.
